title: Quantum Optimization of Currency Arbitrage via Graph-Informed Entanglement Strategies
journal_or_venue: 6th ACM International Conference on AI in Finance (ICAIF '25)
abstract_summary: The paper formulates currency arbitrage with realistic bid and ask rates as a QUBO and evaluates multiple QAOA entanglement strategies under NISQ-like noise. It finds that a graph-centric modular entanglement design (GCME) yields near-optimal solutions (approximation ratio ≈0.999) with minimal optimality gap, demonstrating the benefit of graph-aware circuit design for financial optimization.
methodology_description: The authors formulate currency arbitrage with realistic bid and ask asymmetries as a binary integer program (BIP) and convert it to a QUBO by adding quadratic penalty terms for flow conservation, inflow, and outflow constraints (penalty coefficient λ = 100). Each directed currency-pair is represented by two binary decision variables (bid and ask), producing Q = 2·n·(n−1) variables for an n-currency network. They implement multiple QAOA ansätze differentiated by entanglement/ two-qubit gate patterns: Shifted-Circular-Alternating (SCA), High-Coupling Cycle Entanglement (HCEE), Reduced-Coupling Exploratory Entanglement (RCEE), Midrange-Distance Exploratory Entanglement (MDEE), Same-Bid Reverse Entanglement (SBRE), Bidirectional Symmetric Entanglement Encoding (BSEE), Balanced-Correlation Connectivity Entanglement (BCCE) and Graph-Centric Modular Entanglement (GCME). For each dataset and entanglement design they build the corresponding cost Hamiltonian and standard mixer, run variational optimization of the QAOA parameters, and evaluate performance under a realistic NISQ noise model. Classical CPLEX is used to compute exact optimum values for benchmarking. Experiments are repeated (five runs per configuration) with fixed random seeds to report mean expectation values, approximation ratios and optimality gaps under noise, demonstrating that the graph-centric modular entanglement (GCME) ansatz attains near-optimal solutions with low variance on the tested instances.
experimental_setup: Simulations run on Qiskit's AerSimulator with a custom NISQ noise model using the FakeOsaka backend. Two synthetic FX datasets were used (3-currency and 4-currency networks). 3-currency experiments: 12 qubits, 2-layer QAOA, 8192 shots. 4-currency experiments: 24 qubits, 8-layer QAOA, 131072 shots. Fixed random seeds, COBYLA optimizer, penalty coefficient λ = 100, and five independent runs per configuration. CPLEX provides the exact optimal objective for comparison.
dataset_used: Synthetic foreign-exchange (FX) datasets representing fully connected, bidirectional currency networks with explicit bid and ask rates. Two instances: a 3-currency network and a 4-currency network; bid and ask rate matrices are provided in the paper.
experiment_input: Source: synthetic FX rate matrices defined in the paper. Sizes: 3-currency instance (n=3; QUBO qubits = 12), 4-currency instance (n=4; QUBO qubits = 24). Preprocessing: convert BIP to QUBO by (i) taking log of rates to linearize multiplicative returns, (ii) mapping bid/ask directional decisions to binary variables, (iii) adding squared-penalty quadratic terms for flow/inflow/outflow constraints (λ = 100). No further data cleaning or external datasets reported.
experiment_process: 1) Formulate BIP with bid and ask decision variables and log-return objective. 2) Convert BIP → QUBO by incorporating penalty terms (flow, inflow, outflow) to obtain a quadratic Ising-style cost Hamiltonian. 3) Design multiple QAOA ansätze differing in entanglement/CNOT topology (SCA, HCEE, RCEE, MDEE, SBRE, BSEE, BCCE, GCME). 4) For each ansatz and dataset, initialize QAOA parameters (random for 3-currency; seeded start for 4-currency), set number of layers p (2 for 3-currency, 8 for 4-currency), and run the variational loop using COBYLA to minimize expected cost under the noisy AerSimulator (FakeOsaka noise model). 5) Execute circuits with specified shots (8192 or 131072) and fixed seeds; repeat five times per configuration. 6) Compute metrics (expectation value, approximation ratio, optimality gap) against CPLEX-computed optimum.
experiment_output: Reported outputs per configuration: mean expectation value of the QUBO cost (log-return), approximation ratio (algorithm result / CPLEX optimum), and optimality gap percentage. Results are averaged over five runs with standard deviations reported. Baseline comparisons include standard QAOA and QAOA+SCA; CPLEX optimal values are used as the ground-truth baseline.
reproducibility_notes: The paper specifies datasets (bid/ask matrices for 3- and 4-currency instances), QUBO construction details, penalty coefficients (λ = 100), QAOA layer counts, optimizer (COBYLA), shot counts, simulator (Qiskit AerSimulator) and noise model (FakeOsaka), and reports that fixed seeds were used. However, no code repository, exact random seeds, circuit transpilation/mapping details, or explicit noise model parameters are provided. CPLEX was used to compute exact optima. Overall, the description gives many necessary parameters for reproduction but the absence of released code and exact seeds/noise parameters limits fully deterministic replication.
key_findings: [supported] A Graph-Centric Modular Entanglement (GCME) design for QAOA achieved near-optimal solutions in simulated noisy experiments on 3- and 4-currency bid–ask QUBO instances (approximation ratio ≈ 0.999, optimality gap ≈ 0.01%).

[supported] Incorporating asymmetric bid and ask rates into the QUBO formulation doubles the number of binary variables (qubits) per currency-pair direction and increases Hamiltonian density and two-qubit interactions.

[supported] GCME maintained low variance and near-optimal performance when problem size increased from 12 qubits (3 currencies) to 24 qubits (4 currencies), outperforming other entanglement strategies tested in these simulations.

[supported] Several alternative entanglement strategies (SCA, HCEE, RCEE, MDEE, SBRE, BSEE, BCCE) produce varied results under a realistic noise model, with denser / less graph-aware patterns often more susceptible to noise-induced performance degradation.

[supported] The paper reports quadratic scaling of resource needs for this formulation (qubits Q = 2 n (n − 1) = O(n^2)) and an overall circuit-depth scaling of O(p n^2) for p QAOA layers; this scaling is supported by the reported jump in gates/qubit requirements when moving from 3 to 4 currencies.

[disputed] The introduction asserts that 'arbitrage detection' is NP-complete; this contradicts standard results for negative-cycle detection (e.g., Bellman–Ford solves cycle detection in polynomial time) and is not substantiated within the paper.

[speculative] The authors claim that graph-aware entanglement (GCME) will generalize favorably to substantially larger FX networks (dozens of currencies) and to real quantum hardware; this is proposed as future work and not demonstrated here.

[speculative] The claim that integrating market spread dynamics into quantum optimization 'advances beyond existing arbitrage models' is presented conceptually but not empirically compared to state-of-the-art classical methods beyond reporting CPLEX optima for the test instances.
results_summary: The paper formulates currency arbitrage with explicit bid and ask rates as a QUBO and evaluates QAOA performance under seven entanglement strategies in noisy simulations. GCME, a modular graph-aware entanglement pattern, consistently produced near-optimal results (approx. ratio ≈ 0.999, opt gap ≈ 0.01%) on synthetic 3- and 4-currency datasets (12 and 24 qubits) while other entanglement schemes showed variable performance and higher sensitivity to noise. The work demonstrates that modeling bid–ask asymmetry increases qubit and gate counts (quadratic scaling) and that tailored entanglement topologies can materially affect solution quality on NISQ-like simulations.
performance_claims: GCME: approximation ratio 0.999 ± 0.001 and optimality gap ≈ 0.01% on both 3-currency (expectation -10.003 ± 0.001; CPLEX optimal -10.004) and 4-currency (expectation -10.570 ± 0.003; CPLEX optimal -10.574) datasets. [supported]
Baseline QAOA (3-currency): approximation ratio 0.612 ± 0.475 (expectation -6.126 ± 4.752), opt gap 38.76%. [supported]
Baseline QAOA (4-currency): approximation ratio 0.553 ± 0.463 (expectation -5.852 ± 4.894), opt gap 44.66%. [supported]

Problem encoding requires Q = 2 n (n − 1) qubits for an n-currency network; moving from 3 to 4 currencies doubled qubit count from 12 to 24 and increased circuit depth consistent with O(p n^2) scaling. [supported]
quantum_advantage_detail: The paper presents simulated, small-scale NISQ experiments showing that a tailored entanglement structure (GCME) yields near-optimal solutions for the formulated bid–ask QUBOs. However, it does not demonstrate a computational or practical advantage over classical algorithms (no runtime/speedup comparison, and problem sizes are small and simulated), so any claim of quantum advantage remains speculative.
limitations: Evaluated only small instance sizes (3- and 4-currency networks); results may not generalize to larger FX networks (author-stated).

All experiments were run in simulation (Qiskit AerSimulator with a FakeOsaka noise model) rather than on real quantum hardware, so hardware-specific noise/connectivity effects are not measured (author-stated).
The study assumes fully connected, bidirectional currency graphs and does not model network sparsity or realistic connectivity constraints present on quantum devices (author-stated).

The QUBO conversion enforces constraints via squared penalty terms and a single fixed penalty coefficient (λ=100); this penalty encoding and fixed weight may bias results and requires careful tuning (author-stated).

Circuit depth and gate counts grow rapidly with problem size (qubit count scales as Q = 2 n (n−1) = O(n^2); circuit depth O(p n^2)), creating scalability and NISQ-coherence limitations (author-stated).
Certain entanglement strategies are noise-sensitive and can introduce over-correlations that degrade performance under realistic noise (author-stated).
The cost Hamiltonian becomes denser and more complex after bid–ask modeling (additional linear & quadratic terms), increasing resource demands for simulation and execution (author-stated).
Use of synthetic, static exchange-rate matrices; dynamic market behavior, price slippage, order-book depth, and real execution constraints were not modeled (author-stated/inferred).
[inferred] The formulation maximizes log-returns but does not model trade sizes, liquidity constraints, minimum tick sizes, or market impact which are critical in practical arbitrage.
[inferred] The experiments use a single optimizer (COBYLA), fixed random seeds and a small number of repetitions (five runs), limiting assessment of optimizer sensitivity and statistical robustness.
[inferred] No evaluation of run-time, classical-quantum resource trade-offs, or comparison of wall-clock performance against classical solvers for larger instances was provided.
[inferred] Mapping the QAOA circuits to real-device qubit connectivity (routing, SWAP overhead) and its effect on performance is not addressed.

[inferred] The squared-penalty constraint encoding may create rugged optimization landscapes; alternative constraint encodings (e.g., different quadratizations, Lagrangian approaches) were not explored.
[inferred] The choice of QAOA layer depths (p=2 for 3-currency, p=8 for 4-currency) and initialization strategies were limited; effects of deeper or adaptive p were not systematically studied.

key_ideas: #idea:quantum-advantage — A Graph-Centric Modular Entanglement (GCME) QAOA ansatz achieved near-optimal solutions on tested FX QUBO instances (approximation ratio ≈ 0.999, optimality gap ≈ 0.01%) under the simulated noise model.

#idea:hybrid-approach — The work uses a hybrid variational workflow (QAOA circuits with classical COBYLA optimizer) and classical CPLEX as an exact baseline, demonstrating a practical QPU–CPU style pipeline in simulation.

#idea:near-term-feasibility — Experiments employ a realistic NISQ noise model (FakeOsaka) on Qiskit AerSimulator and report low-variance, near-optimal results for small (12–24 qubit) instances, suggesting potential NISQ-era applicability for toy FX arbitrage problems.

#limitation:qubit-count — The chosen QUBO encoding doubles variables per directed pair yielding Q = 2 * n * (n - 1) qubits (O(n^2) scaling); even modest currency networks rapidly increase qubit requirements.
#limitation:noise — Denser, less graph-aware entanglement patterns suffer more from noise-induced degradation; performance depends on entanglement topology under the applied noise model.
#limitation:simulation-only — All results are from Qiskit AerSimulator with a FakeOsaka noise model (no experiments on real quantum hardware).

#limitation:no-empirical-validation — While many experimental parameters are reported, no code, exact random seeds, or explicit noise parameters/transpilation details are released, limiting fully deterministic reproducibility.

#idea:quantum-advantage — Graph-aware circuit/topology design (GCME) can materially improve QAOA performance on structured financial QUBOs compared to generic entanglement patterns in these small-instance simulations.
